Even if you go into agricultural pursuits with knowledge you still have to prepare your land for it which can take years.
It's amazing how many people don't understand sand/silt/clay ratios or pH.

...depending on the crops you want to plant, the quality of the soil you've got to work with, and the duration of the growing seasons. Working in a community garden and gradually working your way up the learning/experience ladder is still sound starting advice. The writer strikes me as someone who bought a farm seeking independence from the drudgery of urban living with the same thinking people apply to buying a house, which while related are two completely different economic and lifestyle strategies.

Now lets get this out of the way, if someone buys land they intend to put to agriculture use without at least first doing thorough area research, gathering soil samples, and budgeting for hiring, they'll get what they deserve and deserve all that they get, but fortunately most people don't go into industrial concentrated agriculture. At least none that I know of.
I struggle to grow pre-potted tomatoes and believe becoming a raider will be the best plan; for me.
You cannot survive without practice. Doesn't matter if it's planting a seed, raising chickens, or canning applesauce. Start now. Right now.

I chuckled all the way through this article. We've homestead off grid for over a decade and have run into all the problems you described, and then some. We have yet to produce enough food to feed ourselves for a year, although bartering helped some. Another aspect to all that is food storage, which was addressed in a separate post here in the sub. This post has gotten me to think more about gardening that any other I can recall. Why do I suck at gardening? Wrong crops? Wrong soil? Not enough prep? Likely all of the above if not more. I usually in totally reactive fashion start thinking about my garden in April, sometimes May and it's an impulse buy for whatever potted plants are near the checkout at the big box home improvement store. I then put them wherever there is space on my front porch, often with enough sunlight, and then sporadically water them until something edible appears. Once in awhile I actually get enough to make a sandwich with. I am taking a major step back and thinking about what I will do for 2019 now.

First was to take a look at how sunlight went across my yard with this:

suncalc.net

I've been doing it wrong. Instead of placing crops R- L across my yard where they would get full sun throughout the day I've had them top - bottom where they are in shade after a few hours. I've also put in some stakes in my yard for areas that might also be good and tracking how long full sun is in those areas before it goes behind trees.

Pick the best crops for my area...duh! Mostly root vegetables, berries, and some leafy greens. Never tried to grow them however. Decided I should eat some now and see if I actually like them so I've been tracking them down. Sunchokes were a great surprise, absolutely delicious and apparently easy to grow as well as perennial.

Finally, now your growing zone and it will eliminate crop mistakes. Too many seeds I've tried in the past were just on the edge of doing well in my zone and not surprisingly, did not do well. Further, searching your zone on youtube brings up many other gardeners and their wins/fails. I at least feel like I have a chance at getting something decent going next year. Better late than never I suppose.
